paras.t: Pain, numbness, or tingling running down your leg usually starts in your lower back. Casey Morgan D.C. finds where it's coming from before he treats it.

bullets.text: In and out in minutes, not rushed

sections.name: What Section
sections.title: If it runs down your leg, this is the page

paras.t: Sciatica doesn't feel like regular back pain. It shoots, burns, or buzzes down the back of your leg, sometimes all the way to your foot. Some people feel it more as numbness or tingling than pain. Some notice the leg feels weak.
It's often worse sitting, which is a problem if you sit for a living.
Numbness, tingling, and weakness count. A lot of people don't mention them because they don't hurt. Tell Dr. Morgan anyway. They're some of the clearest clues about where the problem is.

sections.name: What Section
sections.title: The pain is in your leg. The problem usually isn't.

paras.t: Sciatica is a symptom, not a diagnosis. It means the sciatic nerve is irritated somewhere along its path, and most of the time that's in the lower back.
The usual cause is a disc that has bulged, herniated, or thinned enough to press on a nerve root. Joints in the lower back that have stopped moving the way they should can add to it.
That's why treating the leg rarely fixes it. You have to find what's pressing on the nerve.

callouts.title: This is why we image before we treat.
callouts.text: Dr. Morgan takes digital X-rays on site when your exam calls for them, reads them himself, and shows them to you the same visit.

sections.title: Find it, fix it, keep it from coming back

paras.t: When we'd send you for an MRI. If you haven't improved after about six weeks, or you finish a plan with less change than expected, Dr. Morgan will refer you for an MRI. That's the next step in finding it, not a failure.

bullets.body: A full history and exam, including how the nerve is behaving: where you feel it, what makes it worse, any numbness or weakness. Digital X-rays if your exam calls for them.

Sciatica usually responds well to adjustments plus spinal decompression, which takes pressure off the disc that's pressing on the nerve. Dr. Morgan recommends decompression when your exam and imaging support it.
Once the problem is corrected, most patients move to maintenance, about once every two weeks. Some stop entirely.

sections.name: First Visit Section
sections.title: Your first visit, start to finish

paras.t: First visit runs about 30 minutes. After that, most visits take a few minutes. Dr. Morgan built the practice around working people.

steps.title: We find out what is actually happening
steps.text: Full history and exam. What hurts, what you have already tried, what you want to get back to doing. Any necessary digital X-rays, taken on site.

steps.title: Dr. Morgan shows you the imaging, same day
steps.text: He marks it up and walks you through it right there. You will see what he sees. Most patients get their first adjustment the same visit.

steps.title: You come back for the full report
steps.text: Within a few days, Dr. Morgan lays out what he found and exactly what he recommends. What it will take, how long, and what it costs. Then you decide.

sections.name: What Section
sections.title: How long until this actually feels better

paras.t: Most people want a number before they start. Dr. Morgan will give you one, just not before he has examined you and looked at your imaging. He will not guess.
What he can tell you up front is how it usually goes, including the part most offices skip: the first two weeks are uneven.
If you are only trying to get out of pain, a shorter plan can do that. If you want it to stay fixed, it takes about 90 days. Dr. Morgan will give you both options and let you pick.

tags.text: Inconsistent, and that's normal. You'll have a good day and think it's fixed, then a bad one and think it's not working. Dr. Morgan warns you about this on day one. Real change usually starts around the end of week two, and better sleep is often the first thing people notice.

The bulk of the plan. A typical plan is about 24 visits over 90 days, two to three times a week at the start, then less often as you improve. Some people need fewer. Dr. Morgan checks your progress along the way.
Most patients move to maintenance, about once every two weeks. Some stop entirely. Dr. Morgan will tell you when you're there.

faqs.q: Why does my leg hurt if the problem is in my back?
faqs.a: The sciatic nerve starts in your lower back and runs down the leg. When something presses on it near the spine, you feel it along the nerve, not where the pressure is.
Not always. Dr. Morgan recommends it when your exam and imaging show a disc pressing on the nerve. It's a cash service, $75 per session, and it always goes alongside your adjustments.

faqs.q: How long until it gets better?
faqs.a: The first week or two are uneven, which is normal. A typical plan is about 24 visits over 90 days. Dr. Morgan gives you a real recommendation on your second visit, after he's looked at everything.

faqs.q: When should I go to the ER instead?
faqs.a: If you lose control of your bladder or bowels, have numbness in your groin or inner thighs, or your leg weakness is getting quickly worse, go to an emergency room. Those can be signs of a serious nerve problem that needs urgent care.
